Well, hi, thank you for seeing me. I guess... well, what brings me in is that my head just feels completely foggy lately. It’s hard to explain, but it’s like I’m walking through mud mentally. I’m a personal care aide, so I’m in and out of clients' houses all day, and I’ve started making these little mistakes in my client notes. Usually, I'm very particular about my notes because the next shift really relies on them to know exactly how the day went, but I'll sit down to write and just completely blank on what happened an hour ago. Or I’ll get up to do something for a client, walk into their kitchen, and just stand there completely forgetting what I was even about to do. 

It’s incredibly frustrating because this really isn’t like me at all. I've always been the organized one, you know? I took some college classes back in the day and always kept on top of my schedule and my responsibilities, so to suddenly have this... this thick fog where I can't even hold onto a simple thought or finish a basic task without second-guessing myself, it’s just really throwing me off. I just keep trying to push through it, but the little mistakes keep happening, and I really can't afford to let my clients down since they rely on me for their daily care, so I figured I had to come in and talk to somebody about it before it gets worse.

Yeah, actually, my sleep has been just... all over the place lately. It's really frustrating. Normally, after a long day of lifting clients and being on my feet, I hit the mattress and I'm out cold. I've always been a good sleeper. But now? I'll get into bed, turn off the lamp, and I just lie there staring at the ceiling. My brain just starts going, mostly thinking about family stuff, you know? I'll toss and turn, flip the pillow over to the cool side, try to get comfortable, but my mind is just stuck on all that family drama. 

And then, even if I do finally manage to drift off, it's not a restful sleep. I end up waking up way before my alarm even goes off. I have my phone set for 5:30 every morning so I have enough time to take a hot shower and make my coffee before I have to drive to my first shift, but lately my eyes will just pop open at 3:45 or 4:00 in the morning. And that's it. I'm just awake. I try to tell myself, "Come on, you have another hour and a half, just close your eyes, you need the rest," but I just can't really settle back down. I'll just lie there in the pitch black, listening to the house creak or the fridge humming in the kitchen, feeling completely exhausted but totally unable to drift off again. It just makes getting through the next day and doing my job feel even more like wading through wet cement, because I'm starting out running on empty.

I mean... I wouldn't say I want to actually do something to myself. I'm not sitting here making a plan or figuring out how to, you know, end it. Even when things got tough with the divorce a few years back, or when my dad got sick, I always kept pushing. I always wanted to be here. I'm not going to hurt myself, I promise I'm not. I mean, reacting to things... no, I wouldn't say there's a difference there either. It's kind of like what I was just saying about moving and talking. My reaction time seems totally fine, even if I feel like garbage on the inside. 

Like, take driving, for instance. I spend half my day in my car, driving from one client's house to the next. And you really have to be on your toes, especially with the way people drive around here lately. Just the other day, maybe Tuesday? I was heading over to Mrs. Gable's house—she's out in the suburbs, usually takes me about twenty-five minutes to get there—and this guy in a silver Honda just completely cut me off. Didn't use his blinker, just swerved right into my lane because he was about to miss his exit. I had to slam on my brakes so hard my work bag went flying off the passenger seat onto the floorboard. My coffee almost spilled everywhere. But I reacted instantly, you know? My foot hit the brake before I even had time to really process what was happening. If my reactions were slowed down, I definitely would have rear-ended him, and then I would have had to deal with the police, insurance, the agency getting mad that I missed a shift... it would have been a whole nightmare. 

So, physically reacting to things, catching things if they fall, hitting the brakes... that's all still sharp. Even with the clients, if someone starts to lose their balance—which happens a lot, especially with the stroke patients—I'm right there, catching them, steadying them, just like I always have. It's just... it's just the mental part. It's the having to get up and do it, the having to care about doing it, that's where the problem is. But the actual physical wiring? The reflexes? No, I haven't noticed any delay with that at all. It's all still working the way it's supposed to, even if the rest of me feels like it's shutting down.

No... no, I haven't lost any weight, not that I've noticed anyway. You'd think with how exhausting everything feels, maybe I wouldn't have the appetite to eat, but honestly, my weight has stayed pretty much exactly the same.

Well, I guess... I mean, yes, in terms of the toll it takes on me, absolutely. Like I was just saying, I can physically get up and do the work, I don't have a problem getting the motor running, so to speak. But the sheer amount of energy it drains from me? It's ridiculous.

I'm just totally depleted.

So yeah, the effort required for just... just normal, everyday things, it's exhausting. I can start the task, sure, because I have to, but I'm just so tired all the time, even when I haven't really done anything to earn it.

I'm not going to hurt myself, I promise I'm not. He's a pretty big guy, probably around 220 pounds, and he's completely bedbound, so getting him up and ready for the day is a whole physical production. But I walk in there at 8 AM sharp, put my bag down, wash my hands at the kitchen sink—because his daughter is really particular about germs, which I totally get, you know, you can never be too careful—and I just get right to it. There's no hesitation or standing around trying to get my body to work. I just roll him over, get the Hoyer lift sling tucked under his back, hook up the chains, and pump the handle. \n\nAnd you have to move at a pretty good clip, too, because it's really uncomfortable for them to just be hanging there in the sling while you maneuver the machine. That carpet in his bedroom is this thick, awful shag from the seventies, so you really have to put your back into pushing the wheels to get him over to the commode. If I was moving slower than normal, or if I couldn't initiate the movements right away, it would take all morning just to get him into his wheelchair, and it would completely throw off my schedule. I usually have three more people to see before lunch, so I have to keep a steady pace. \n\nSo physically? No. My body moves exactly the same way it always has, at the exact same speed. Like I was saying earlier, I might not have the mental drive to cook a meal when I get home, and I might just sit in my recliner because I'm mentally exhausted, but the actual physical mechanism of getting up and moving? It's totally fine. I might be forty-three and a little stiff in the knees when it rains, but I'm definitely not moving any slower than I used to, and I don't have any trouble physically starting a task once it's time to do it.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like it takes you a lot of effort to start doing something, even if it's a small task?\n\nPatient: Well, I guess... I mean, yes, in terms of the toll it takes on me, absolutely. Like I was just saying, I can physically get up and do the work, I don't have a problem getting the motor running, so to speak. But the sheer amount of energy it drains from me? It's ridiculous. \n\nIt’s just this deep, heavy feeling in my bones. Even on my days off, like on a Sunday when I don't have any clients scheduled and I literally don't do much of anything besides sit in that recliner I told you about, my body just feels completely worn out. Take helping a client with a shower, for instance. I'm just totally depleted. \n\nOr even just my own errands, like carrying groceries into the house. Just grabbing two or three bags and walking up the three steps to my front porch feels like this monumental effort.
